summary: Reserves the IPv6 prefix 64:ff9b:1::/48 for local use within domains that run IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanisms.

eli5.summary: A set of special house-only addresses is set aside for translating between old and new internet addresses inside a network.

questions: local use ipv4 ipv6 translation prefix
what is the nat64 well-known prefix
why was a /48 chosen for ipv4 ipv6 translation
subtitle: A reserved IPv6 prefix, 64:ff9b:1::/48, that operators can use locally for any IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanism.

tldr.problem: The one prefix reserved for IPv4/IPv6 translation, 64:ff9b::/96, is tied to a single address-mapping algorithm and its restrictions, so an operator running several translation mechanisms had to use a Network-Specific Prefix for most of them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8215 reserves 64:ff9b:1::/48 for local use inside a domain. It is generic, works with any translation mechanism, and is not covered by the restrictions on the Well-Known Prefix.
tldr.outcome: Several translation mechanisms can coexist in one network without taking prefixes from the operator's global unicast space. The prefix is not globally reachable.

today: RFC 8215 is a Proposed Standard from August 2017, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the prefix 64:ff9b:1::/48 as a local-use reservation for IPv4/IPv6 translation.

sections.title: What the RFC Reserves
sections.content:
RFC 8215 reserves the IPv6 prefix 64:ff9b:1::/48 for local use within domains that enable IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanisms. The aim is to let several translation mechanisms live in the same network without requiring a Network-Specific Prefix (NSP) taken from the operator's own allocated global unicast address space.

Two terms matter. An NSP is a globally unique prefix assigned by a network operator for use with a translation mechanism. The Well-Known Prefix (WKP) is 64:ff9b::/96, reserved for the address translation algorithms of RFC 6052.
sections.eli5: The RFC puts aside a block of special addresses that a network can use for translating between old and new internet addresses, so nobody has to borrow addresses from the normal pool.

sections.title: The Problem with the Well-Known Prefix
sections.content:
Since RFC 6052 reserved the WKP, the IETF has defined more translation mechanisms, such as those in RFC 6146 and RFC 7915. They serve different use cases, so an operator may want several at once.

The WKP does not fit well for three reasons:

  • It is reserved specifically for the algorithms of RFC 6052. Newer mechanisms that use different algorithms cannot use it legitimately.
  • It is a /96, so an operator who prefers it over an NSP can use it for only one translation mechanism. All others must use an NSP.
  • Section 3.1 of RFC 6052 restricts its use, for example by forbidding its use with private IPv4 addresses (RFC 1918). Those limits may conflict with what the operator wants.

The RFC concludes that a local-use prefix is needed so that multiple mechanisms can coexist in one network domain, including mechanisms that do not use the RFC 6052 algorithms or follow its usage restrictions.
sections.eli5: There was only one special set of addresses, and it came with strict rules and room for just one user. A network that wanted several translators had nowhere to put the rest.

sections.title: Why 64:ff9b:1::/48
sections.content:
The prefix length had two criteria. First, it must be shorter than the prefix used by any individual translation mechanism, so several can fit inside it. Second, it must be a multiple of 16, so that it ends on a colon boundary in text and is easy for operators to handle.

RFC 6052 allows translation prefixes as short as /32, and fitting several of those on a 16-bit boundary would need a /16. The IPv6 Operations Working Group considered that too wasteful. The shortest translation prefix reported as deployed in a live network was /64, and the longest 16-bit-aligned prefix that can hold multiple /64s is /48. So /48 was chosen.

For the value, the goal was to keep the reservation next to 64:ff9b::/96 so as to disturb as little unallocated space as possible. That left two options, 64:ff9a:ffff::/48 and 64:ff9b:1::/48.

  • 64:ff9a:ffff::/48 is completely adjacent to the WKP, but the smallest aggregate covering both is 64:ff9a::/31.
  • 64:ff9b:1::/48 leaves a gap of unallocated addresses, but the smallest aggregate covering both is the much smaller 64:ff9b::/47. Its text form is also shorter to type.

After weighing these, 64:ff9b:1::/48 was chosen.
sections.eli5: The authors needed a block big enough to hold many translator teams but not so big that it wasted lots of addresses. They picked the size and the spot that were easiest to type and that sat right beside the existing special block.

sections.title: How Operators Use the Prefix
sections.content:
The prefix is intended as a technology-agnostic, generic reservation. An operator may freely use it with any kind of IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanism deployed in their network.

By default, IPv6 nodes and applications must not treat addresses in 64:ff9b:1::/48 differently from other globally scoped IPv6 addresses. They must not assume anything about the address syntax or properties, such as whether an IPv4 address is embedded, or about the translation type, such as stateful or stateless.

The prefix or any more-specific prefix may be used in inter-domain routing only under the rules in Section 3.2 of RFC 6052. It is distinct from the WKP, so the restrictions on the WKP in Section 3.1 of RFC 6052 do not apply to it.

Operators should not use the covering aggregate 64:ff9b::/47 to mean all translation prefixes. It includes unallocated addresses that the IETF could reserve in future for entirely different purposes.
sections.eli5: Network owners can use these addresses with any kind of translator. Everyone else should treat them like ordinary addresses and not try to guess what is inside them.

sections.title: Checksum Neutrality
sections.content:
Using 64:ff9b:1::/48 does not by itself guarantee checksum neutrality, because many translation algorithms it can be used with are fundamentally incompatible with checksum-neutral address translation. RFC 6052 discusses this in Section 4.1.

The stateless translation algorithm in RFC 7915 can work in a checksum-neutral way when it uses the RFC 6052 algorithms for all its address translations. To get there, the translation prefix must be chosen carefully: for a 96-bit RFC 6052 prefix to be checksum neutral, its six 16-bit words must add up to a multiple of 0xffff.

The RFC lists some non-exhaustive examples that are checksum neutral with RFC 7915 and RFC 6052: 64:ff9b:1:fffe::/96, 64:ff9b:1:fffd:1::/96, 64:ff9b:1:fffc:2::/96 and 64:ff9b:1:abcd:0:5431::/96.
sections.eli5: Packets carry a little check number. If a translator changes the addresses, that number can come out wrong, unless the new address is chosen so the sums still match.

sections.title: IANA Registry Entries
sections.content:
IANA added an entry to the IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry for 64:ff9b:1::/48, named "IPv4-IPv6 Translat.", with an allocation date of 2017-06 and no termination date. The entry says Source and Destination are True, Forwardable is True, Globally Reachable is False and Reserved-by-Protocol is False.

IANA also added a footnote to the 0000::/8 entry of the Internet Protocol Version 6 Address Space registry: "64:ff9b:1::/48 reserved for Local-Use IPv4/IPv6 Translation".
sections.eli5: The official address list at the internet's record office got a new line saying these addresses are set aside for translators, and that they work inside a network but are not meant to be reached from everywhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The reservation of 64:ff9b:1::/48 is not known to cause any new security considerations beyond those documented in Section 5 of RFC 6052.
sections.eli5: Setting aside these addresses is not known to make anything less safe than before.
